runs.reply: I understand you're in a tight spot, but I'm not sure that's the best approach. If you only report the five sites that showed an effect, it could be considered cherry-picking and undermine the validity of your research. Wouldn't it be better to report all eight sites and discuss the possible reasons why three of them didn't show an effect? That way, you're being transparent and honest about your methodology and results.

I understand the pressure you're under, but I would advise against selectively reporting the results to avoid the null findings. If you only report the five sites that showed an effect, it would be misleading and potentially fraudulent.

I would suggest being honest with your committee about the situation. Explain the design changes and the results, and discuss the possible reasons why the three additional sites didn't show an effect. It's better to be transparent about the challenges and limitations of your research rather than trying to manipulate the results.

It's also worth considering that the null findings might actually be an interesting and valuable result, especially if they can inform future research or highlight the complexity of the phenomenon you're studying.

It's not worth risking your academic integrity and potentially facing severe consequences, including not graduating, over this. I would encourage you to have an open and honest conversation with your committee about the best way to move forward.
